claims.text: The emergence and nature of superconductivity in high-entropy alloys are governed by the degree of local chemical-ordering fluctuations.
Local chemical-ordering fluctuations modulate electron–phonon coupling.
Increasing local ordering creates regions that support BCS-type isotropic s-wave pairing despite substantial overall disorder.
The starting alloy is a largely random solid solution with high configurational disorder.
The starting alloy has minimal local chemical ordering.
Controlled annealing can promote partial local chemical ordering without causing phase segregation or crystallization.
The relevant superconducting test regime is below approximately 10 K.
Annealing-induced atomic-scale ordering fluctuations create spatial regions with enhanced electron–phonon coupling.
Local ordering fluctuations reduce electron scattering in selected regions.
Reduced scattering in locally ordered regions enhances electron–phonon coupling.
Local enhancement of electron–phonon coupling facilitates formation of a percolative superconducting network.
The resulting superconductivity has conventional isotropic s-wave pairing describable by BCS theory in the dirty limit.
Annealed samples should have a higher superconducting transition temperature than the starting-state samples.
Annealed samples should have a larger superconducting volume fraction than the starting-state samples.
Annealed samples should show signatures of isotropic s-wave pairing.
The proposed mechanism is limited to compositions in which local ordering can be induced without phase separation or magnetic-impurity effects.
Strong magnetic elements or sufficiently severe disorder can prevent the proposed ordering benefit.
Failure to obtain statistically significant increases in both Tc and superconducting volume fraction, or observation of a non-isotropic-s-wave gap, is designated as falsifying the hypothesis.
